b: Volume overload : Decreased GFR → sodium and water retention; impaired natriuresis — Rising weight, bibasal crackles, peripheral oedema, pleural effusion on CXR — Increases risk of pulmonary oedema, prolongs ICU stay; a trigger for early di

Electrolyte derangements – hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, hyponatraemia : Reduced tubular secretion (K⁺, H⁺) and impaired free water clearance — Serum K⁺ 6 mmol/L, arterial pH < 7.2, serum Na⁺ < 130 mmol/L — Hyperkalaemia is the commone

Uraemic encephalopathy / pericarditis : Accumulation of nitrogenous waste products and inflammatory mediators — Altered mental status, asterixis, pericardial rub, diffuse ST‑segment changes — Marks progression to stage 3 AKI; mortality rise

Infection (catheter‑related sepsis, pneumonia) : Immunomodulation by uremia, loss of barrier function, invasive lines — New fever, leukocytosis, purulent drainage from catheter — Sepsis can precipitate a second hit to the kidney, converting

Acute kidney disease (AKD) : Incomplete recovery within 7 days but 48 h after insult — Persistently rising creatinine beyond day 3, urine output still <0.5 mL/kg/h — AKD is a strong predictor of transition to chronic kidney disease (CKD); e

Mitral stenosis : ↑ left atrial pressure → pulmonary venous congestion — Atrial fibrillation, thrombo‑embolism, right‑sided heart failure, pulmonary hypertension — Progressive dyspnoea; symptom‑limited survival improves markedly after percu

Mitral regurgitation (chronic) : Volume overload of left ventricle → eccentric hypertrophy — Progressive LV dilation, systolic dysfunction, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary oedema — Asymptomatic patients have long latent period; once EF falls

Aortic stenosis (calcific) : Fixed outflow obstruction → LV pressure overload — LV concentric hypertrophy, myocardial ischaemia, syncope, sudden cardiac death, heart failure — Once mean gradient 40 mmHg or symptoms develop, median survival

Aortic regurgitation (chronic) : Diastolic run‑off → LV volume overload — LV dilation, reduced EF, aortic root dilatation, end‑aortic dissection (in Marfan or bicuspid valve), infective endocarditis — Asymptomatic patients may remain stable

Tricuspid regurgitation (functional) : Systemic venous congestion — Hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral oedema, right‑sided failure — Often a marker of advanced left‑sided disease; prognosis tied to underlying cause rather than regurgitation

Acute bacterial super‑infection (pneumonia) : Disruption of mucociliary clearance and viral‑induced epithelial injury allow bacterial colonisation of distal airways — New focal crackles, fever 38 °C, tachypnoea, pleuritic pain; may require

Post‑infectious cough : Persistent airway hyper‑reactivity and mucus gland irritation after viral clearance — Cough lasting 3 weeks, often dry, may respond to inhaled bronchodilator or low‑dose steroid — 3–8 weeks after onset

Exacerbation of underlying asthma or COPD : Inflammatory mediators (IL‑6, TNF‑α) amplify bronchial smooth‑muscle tone — Worsening wheeze, dyspnoea, fall in FEV₁, possible need for systemic steroids — Can occur during the acute bout or short

Cor pulmonale (in chronic bronchitis) : Chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction → pulmonary arterial hypertension → right‑ventricular overload — Peripheral oedema, raised JVP, hepatomegaly; predicts higher mortality — Develops over years of untrea

Secondary bacterial infection of the lower airway (bronchiectasis) : Recurrent inflammation damages bronchial wall, impairs clearance, leading to permanent dilatation — Daily sputum, frequent exacerbations, haemoptysis; radiological bronchi

Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF) : Coalescence of nodules → dense collagenous mass, usually in upper zones (silica, coal) or lower zones (asbestos) — Severe restrictive defect, hypoxaemia, right‑heart strain, high mortality — 5–15 yr afte

Silico‑tuberculosis : Silica impairs macrophage killing, facilitates Mycobacterium tuberculosis replication — Chronic cough, weight loss, cavitary disease; synergistic increase in mortality — Often within 2–10 yr of silicosis diagnosis

Pulmonary hypertension : Chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction + loss of capillary bed from fibrosis — Exertional dyspnoea out of proportion to spirometry, right‑sided edema — Late stage, 10–20 yr after disease onset

Lung cancer : Carcinogenic dust (silica, asbestos, diesel) + chronic inflammation — New infiltrate, weight loss, haemoptysis; prognosis poorer than idiopathic lung cancer — 15–30 yr latency; risk proportional to cumulative exposure

Malignant mesothelioma : Asbestos fibres provoke chronic pleural inflammation → mesothelial transformation — Pleural effusion, chest pain, weight loss; median survival < 12 months — 20–40 yr after asbestos exposure

ai.title: Complications and Prognosis in Acute Kidney Injury
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute kidney injury (AKI) can progress to volume overload, electrolyte derangements, uraemic encephalopathy, infection and chronic kidney disease. Recognising these complications early guides urgent management and informs prognosis, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: AKI is a sudden decline in kidney function defined by KDIGO: increase in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h or ≥1.5‑fold from baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h.
b: KDIGO criteria allow staging even when baseline labs are missing.
In low‑resource hospitals, urine output and bedside assessment of fluid balance are often the first clues.

sections.p: KDIGO stages I‑III use creatinine rise and urine output. Stage III (creatinine ≥3 × baseline or ≥4 mg/dL, or anuria >12 h) carries the highest mortality.
b: Stage III predicts need for renal replacement therapy (RRT).
Stage I may still progress if underlying cause not addressed.

sections.p: In East African hospitals the common precipitants are:
b: Sepsis from malaria, typhoid, or catheter‑related infections.
Volume depletion from diarrhoea, vomiting, or diuretic over‑use.
Nephrotoxins: aminoglycosides, traditional herbal remedies, NSAIDs.
Obstructive uropathy from stones or prostatic enlargement.

sections.p: Patients may have oliguria, peripheral oedema, rising weight, and symptoms of uremia such as nausea, asterixis, or confusion.
b: New crackles at lung bases suggest volume overload.
Peripheral edema with raised jugular venous pressure points to fluid retention.

t.b: Is kidney function falling? A rise ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 h confirms AKI.
Is the patient oliguric? <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h indicates stage II‑III.
Are dangerous derangements present? K⁺ ≥6 mmol/L or HCO₃⁻ <15 mmol/L signals need for urgent correction.
Is there renal cortical thickening or obstruction? Absence of flow suggests post‑renal cause.

sections.p: Complications drive mortality and dictate escalation of care.
b: Volume overload → pulmonary oedema, pleural effusion, worsening hypoxia.
Hyperkalaemia ≥6 mmol/L → ventricular arrhythmia risk.
Metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2) → respiratory compromise.
Uraemic encephalopathy → altered mental status, asterixis.
Catheter‑related sepsis → new fever, leukocytosis, purulent drainage.

sections.p: Treat the precipitant, control fluid/electrolyte balance, and consider renal replacement when indicated.
b: Stop nephrotoxins; switch aminoglycosides to safer alternatives.
Give isotonic saline cautiously if hypovolaemic; avoid fluid overload in stage II‑III.
Use calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, or sodium bicarbonate for hyperkalaemia; avoid diuretics if volume depleted.
Dialysis (peritoneal or intermittent haemodialysis) is preferred when K⁺ ≥6 mmol/L, pH <7.2, or refractory fluid overload.
Treat infection promptly with empiric antibiotics covering local pathogens (e.g., ceftriaxone for typhoid, artesunate for severe malaria).

sections.p: After AKI resolution, monitor for chronic kidney disease (CKD) and educate on avoidance of repeat insults.
b: Re‑measure creatinine at 7 days and 3 months; a persistent rise predicts CKD.
Educate on safe use of herbal medicines and NSAIDs.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus to reduce future infections.
Acute decompensated heart failure – both cause pulmonary crackles, but heart failure shows elevated JVP and peripheral edema without rising creatinine.
Severe malaria‑induced hemolysis – may cause AKI but also shows high bilirubin and parasite smear.
Serum creatinine may be normal in early AKI if muscle mass is low; rely on urine output.
Potassium can be falsely low if the sample is hemolysed; repeat if clinical picture suggests hyperkalaemia.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain with new pulmonary crackles and oxygen saturation <90 %
K⁺ ≥6 mmol/L or pH <7.2 despite treatment

faq.q: Why does AKI cause pulmonary oedema?
faq.a: Reduced GFR leads to sodium and water retention, raising hydrostatic pressure in pulmonary capillaries and causing fluid leak into alveoli.
Yes, if the underlying cause is removed and fluid/electrolyte derangements are corrected, many patients recover, especially in stage I‑II.

faq.q: What is the difference between AKI and AKD?
faq.a: AKI is the initial injury (≤7 days); AKD describes incomplete recovery between day 3 and day 7, signalling higher risk of chronic kidney disease.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with malaria presents with oliguria and K⁺ 6.5 mmol/L – what is your immediate management and why? — Give calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, consider dialysis; explain each step prevents arrhythmia.
How does volume overload in AKI differ from heart‑failure‑related overload on examination? — Highlight JVP, peripheral edema pattern, and lack of S3 in pure AKI.
A patient on traditional herbal medicine develops AKI; which toxin is most likely and how would you counsel? — Discuss aristolochic acid risk, advise cessation and safe alternatives.
Why is urine output more reliable than creatinine in early AKI in a malnourished patient? — Explain low muscle mass blunts creatinine rise; oliguria signals reduced filtration.
What red‑flag laboratory value mandates urgent dialysis in AKI? — K⁺ ≥6 mmol/L, pH <7.2, or refractory fluid overload; justify based on mortality data.
Distinguish AKI caused by sepsis from that caused by hypovolaemia on bedside assessment. — Look for fever, warm extremities, capillary refill, versus dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, low CVP.
Explain how AKI predisposes to catheter‑related sepsis. — Uraemia impairs neutrophil function and barrier integrity, increasing infection risk.
What follow‑up plan would you give a patient discharged after stage II AKI? — Repeat creatinine at 7 days and 3 months, advise hydration, avoid nephrotoxins, and schedule CKD screening.
